items.title: AI Development
items.summary: Language model features that do real work in a product, rather than a demo nobody uses.
problems: The AI demo impressed everyone, but it is not connected to your real data or your real workflow, so it stayed a demo.
Your team spends hours a week on repetitive work that a properly scoped model call could handle safely.
You want AI in the product, but your customer data cannot leave your own infrastructure.
audience: Product teams adding an AI feature to an application that already has users.
Founders building an AI-first product from the beginning.
Teams with a manual process that keeps growing faster than the headcount.
deliverables: A model integration behind a clean interface, with timeouts, retries, output validation and a hard cost ceiling.
Retrieval over your own documents and data, so answers come from your content instead of from the model's memory.
Agent workflows that run as background jobs and report what they did, including when they failed.
Provider abstraction, so the model can be swapped for a cheaper or self-hosted one without touching the product.
outcomes: A working feature in production, with guardrails and a cost you can predict per month.
A clear answer on which parts of your process should be automated and which should stay human.

items.title: Backend Development
items.summary: The part that has to hold up: data model, APIs, background jobs, and the deployment that keeps them running.
problems: The product works fine until traffic, data volume or a second developer arrives.
Nobody wants to change the database, because nobody is sure what will break.
Integrations with partners or older systems are still done by hand, by one person who knows how.
audience: Companies whose backend has outgrown the design it started with.
Teams that need an API for a mobile app, a partner or an integration.
Products where correctness matters more than shipping features quickly.
deliverables: Schema design and migrations that can be run repeatedly without a panic.
REST APIs documented well enough that another team can integrate without a call.
Background processing for anything that should not block a user request.
Containerised deployment with a reproducible build and a way back if a release goes wrong.
outcomes: A backend another engineer can pick up without a long handover.
Deployments that are boring, which is the point.

items.title: Mobile Development
items.summary: Apps for Android and iOS, built by someone who has shipped to both stores and dealt with what they reject.
problems: The app exists as a prototype but has never been through a store review.
A cross-platform build is fighting the platform instead of using it.
The project stalled on device integration: Bluetooth, camera, sensors or offline storage.
audience: Businesses that need an app alongside the product their customers already use.
Teams adding a mobile client to a backend that is already in place.
Founders who need one codebase covering both platforms.
deliverables: Android in Kotlin and iOS in Swift, or one React Native codebase where that is the honest choice.
Offline-first storage and sync, for apps used where the connection is not reliable.
Release pipelines: signed builds, versioning, and a working path to the stores.
Device features, including Bluetooth, camera capture and document scanning.
outcomes: An app in the stores, or a build you can install and test with real users straight away.
A native-or-cross-platform decision made from your feature list, not from fashion.

items.title: Full-Stack Product Development
items.summary: The whole product: the idea, the architecture, the interface, the backend, the deployment and the first release.
problems: The idea is clear, but the path from it to a running product is not.
The MVP was built by three people at different times and the pieces no longer fit together.
You need a technical partner who can make decisions and then build, without a team to manage.
audience: Founders taking a product from an idea to its first real users.
Small companies replacing a spreadsheet-and-email process with software.
Businesses with an internal tool that nobody wants to be responsible for.
deliverables: A working first version, cut down to the smallest feature set that proves the idea.
Architecture and infrastructure sized to the load you actually have, not to a hypothetical one.
A web application plus the admin side that always turns out to be needed.
Documentation and a handover that leaves you able to continue without me.
outcomes: Something you can put in front of users and improve from there.
A codebase and a deployment you own, rather than one you rent.

about.metaTitle: About — Software Engineer, 8+ Years of Production Systems
about.metaDescription: Eight years of backend, mobile and AI work: financial systems, distributed services, and complete products taken from idea to production.
about.heading: Eight years of shipping software that has to keep working
about.lead: I started in 2018 on financial systems in Java, moved through distributed backends and marketplaces, and now build products end to end, with AI where it genuinely helps. I have stayed responsible for systems after release in every role, which changes how you build them.
story: My first years were finance software at Crossinx, where a wrong number is a real problem. That is where I learned to design the schema before writing the feature, to treat a migration as something that has to be reversible, and to test the paths nobody clicks. Java and Spring Boot were the tools; care with data was the lesson.

Amdaris moved me into distributed systems: Kafka, GraphQL, services owned by different teams, and deployments to Azure. At FeelIT I worked closer to the product itself, including the first language model features I put into production. Today I am the only developer on three products at once, which means the design, the code, the releases and the support are all mine.

principles.title: Data first
principles.body: Most of the hard problems in a product live in its data, not in its screens. I spend the early part of a project on the schema, the states a record can be in, and what happens when two people change the same thing at once. That is what makes later features cheap instead of painful.

principles.title: Own it after release
principles.body: I have been the only developer on three products at once: writing the features, running the builds, publishing the releases and answering the problems afterwards. That removes the gap where something counts as done but does not actually work, and it is why I care about release pipelines as much as about code.

principles.title: AI with guardrails
principles.body: A model call is a dependency with unpredictable latency, real cost and a habit of being confidently wrong. So I put timeouts, output validation, a token budget and a fallback in front of every integration, and I measure what it costs before it has to scale.

principles.title: Runnable by someone else
principles.body: Documentation, tests and a deployment another engineer can repeat are not extras. They are the difference between a project you can continue without me and one you cannot, and you should be able to leave whenever you want.
